description: Anatomy knowledge base for the Simtack body map. One chunk per region. The retriever uses this with simple cosine similarity over a bag-of-words embedding (see app/services/anatomy_retriever.py). The LLM in /anatomy/ask uses the retrieved chunks as grounded context.

regions.text: Pain in the cranial region can involve the skull, scalp, meninges, blood vessels, and the upper cervical nerves. Common causes include tension-type headache, migraine, cluster headache, sinusitis, and high blood pressure. Red flags include sudden severe worst-ever headache, fever, neck stiffness, neurological deficits, or a headache after head injury.
red_flags: Sudden worst headache of life
Fever with neck stiffness
New neurological deficit
Headache after head injury
suggested_questions: When did the headache start?
Is it on one side or both?
Any nausea, vomiting, or visual changes?
Any recent head injury?

regions.text: Neck pain may arise from muscles, cervical spine, lymph nodes, or the thyroid. Common causes include muscle strain, cervical spondylosis, lymphadenitis from infection, and thyroiditis. Red flags include severe pain after trauma, neurological symptoms in arms, fever, or a hard fixed mass.
red_flags: Severe pain after trauma
Arm weakness or numbness
Fever with tender lymph nodes
Hard fixed neck mass
suggested_questions: Any recent injury or strain?
Pain radiates to shoulders or arms?
Any fever or sore throat?
Any swelling you can feel?

regions.text: Chest pain can be cardiac, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, or gastrointestinal. Cardiac causes include angina and myocardial infarction. Pulmonary causes include pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and pneumonia. Musculoskeletal causes include costochondritis and rib injury. Red flags include crushing central chest pain, pain radiating to left arm or jaw, shortness of breath, sweating, and fainting.
red_flags: Crushing central chest pain
Radiation to left arm or jaw
Shortness of breath
Fainting or near-fainting
suggested_questions: Is the pain sharp, dull, or crushing?
Does it spread to arm, jaw, or back?
Any shortness of breath?
Any sweating or nausea with it?

regions.text: Upper abdominal pain may come from the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, or spleen. Common causes include gastritis, peptic ulcer, gallstones, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, and hepatitis. Red flags include severe sudden pain, jaundice, vomiting blood, or black tarry stools.
red_flags: Severe sudden pain
Yellowing of skin or eyes
Vomiting blood or black stools
Pain radiating to right shoulder
suggested_questions: When did the pain start?
Any nausea or vomiting?
Any change in stool color?
Pain after fatty meals?

structures: Right ovary and fallopian tube (in females)
regions.text: Right lower abdominal pain is classically associated with appendicitis, especially when pain starts near the navel and moves to the right lower quadrant. Other causes include right ovarian cyst, ectopic pregnancy, kidney stone, and Crohn's disease. Red flags include severe pain with fever, rigid abdomen, and fainting.
red_flags: Pain migrating from navel to right lower quadrant
Fever with abdominal pain
Rigid abdomen
Positive pregnancy test with pain
suggested_questions: Did the pain start near the navel?
Any fever?
Any change in bowel habits?
Last menstrual period (if applicable)?

structures: Left ovary and fallopian tube (in females)
regions.text: Left lower abdominal pain commonly comes from the sigmoid colon, left ovary, or left ureter. Common causes include diverticulitis, constipation, ovarian cyst, ectopic pregnancy, and kidney stone. Red flags include severe pain with fever, blood in stool, or fainting.
red_flags: Severe pain with fever
Blood in stool
Positive pregnancy test with pain
Fainting
suggested_questions: Any change in bowel habits?
Any blood in stool?
Any fever?
Last menstrual period (if applicable)?

regions.text: Hip and groin pain may come from the hip joint, muscles, inguinal hernia, or pelvic structures. Common causes include hip osteoarthritis, muscle strain, inguinal hernia, and kidney stone referred pain. Red flags include inability to bear weight, severe pain after fall, or a new bulge in the groin.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight
Severe pain after fall
New bulge in groin
Fever with hip pain
suggested_questions: Any recent injury?
Can you bear weight on the leg?
Any bulge in the groin area?
Any fever?

regions.text: Thigh pain can come from muscles, the femur, or blood vessels. Common causes include muscle strain, contusion, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and stress fracture. Red flags include sudden swelling, calf pain, warmth, and discoloration suggestive of DVT.
red_flags: Sudden leg swelling
Calf pain and warmth
Skin redness or discoloration
Pain after long immobilization
suggested_questions: Any recent injury or strain?
Any leg swelling?
Any recent long travel or bed rest?
Any calf pain?

regions.text: Upper back pain often comes from muscles, thoracic spine, or referred pain from the lungs or heart. Common causes include muscle strain, thoracic spine dysfunction, and pleurisy. Red flags include pain with shortness of breath, severe pain after trauma, or neurological deficits.
red_flags: Pain with shortness of breath
Severe pain after trauma
Numbness or weakness in legs
Loss of bladder or bowel control
suggested_questions: Any recent strain or injury?
Any shortness of breath?
Any numbness or tingling?
Any fever?

regions.text: Lower back pain is extremely common. Causes include muscle strain, disc herniation, sciatica, kidney stones, and pyelonephritis. Red flags include loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin, severe pain after trauma, or pain with fever.
red_flags: Loss of bladder or bowel control
Numbness in groin or inner thighs
Severe pain after trauma
Pain with fever
suggested_questions: Any recent strain or injury?
Does pain radiate down the leg?
Any numbness or weakness?
Any fever or urinary symptoms?

regions.text: Right arm and shoulder pain can be musculoskeletal, neurological, or referred from the neck, gallbladder, or diaphragm. Common causes include rotator cuff tendinopathy, adhesive capsulitis, cervical radiculopathy, and gallbladder referred pain. Red flags include sudden severe chest or arm pain with shortness of breath.
red_flags: Sudden chest and arm pain with shortness of breath
Visible deformity after injury
Loss of arm sensation
Severe pain with no movement
suggested_questions: Any recent injury?
Can you lift the arm?
Any neck pain?
Any abdominal pain?

regions.text: Left arm and shoulder pain may be musculoskeletal, but it is also a classic site of referred cardiac pain. Chest pain radiating to the left arm is a red flag for myocardial infarction. Other causes include rotator cuff tendinopathy and cervical radiculopathy. Always rule out cardiac causes first.
red_flags: Chest pain with left arm pain
Shortness of breath
Sweating or nausea with arm pain
Sudden severe arm pain with coldness
suggested_questions: Any chest pain with the arm pain?
Any shortness of breath?
Any recent injury?
Any neck pain?

regions.text: Right leg and knee pain commonly comes from the knee joint, muscles, or referred pain. Common causes include meniscal tear, ligament sprain, osteoarthritis, deep vein thrombosis, and Baker's cyst. Red flags include inability to bear weight, sudden severe swelling, or a hot tender calf.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight
Sudden severe swelling
Hot tender calf
Locked knee
suggested_questions: Any recent injury?
Can you bear weight on the leg?
Any calf swelling or pain?
Any locking or giving way?

regions.text: Left leg and knee pain shares the same causes as the right side, with the addition of possible referred pain from the left lower abdomen or pelvis. Common causes include meniscal tear, ligament sprain, osteoarthritis, DVT, and kidney stone referred pain. Red flags include inability to bear weight, sudden severe swelling, or blood in urine.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight
Sudden severe swelling
Hot tender calf
Blood in urine
suggested_questions: Any recent injury?
Can you bear weight on the leg?
Any calf swelling or pain?
Any urinary symptoms?

structures: Rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, teres minor)
regions.text: Right shoulder pain is usually musculoskeletal, from the rotator cuff, the joint itself, or surrounding tendons, but can occasionally be referred from the gallbladder via the phrenic nerve. Common causes include rotator cuff tendinopathy, shoulder impingement, frozen shoulder, and AC joint sprain. Red flags include sudden pain after a fall with visible deformity, complete inability to move the arm, or numbness spreading down the arm.
red_flags: Visible deformity after a fall or injury
Complete inability to move the arm
Numbness or tingling down the arm
Severe pain with fever (possible joint infection)
suggested_questions: Any recent injury or fall?
Can you raise your arm above your head?
Any numbness or tingling down the arm?
Any right upper abdominal pain along with it?

structures: Rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, teres minor)
regions.text: Left shoulder pain is usually musculoskeletal, but the left shoulder is also a classic site of referred cardiac pain: chest pain radiating to the left shoulder or arm is a red flag for a heart attack. Other causes include rotator cuff tendinopathy, shoulder impingement, and frozen shoulder. Always ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea alongside left shoulder pain before assuming it is purely musculoskeletal.
red_flags: Chest pain, tightness, or pressure with the shoulder pain
Shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea
Visible deformity after a fall or injury
Numbness or tingling down the arm
suggested_questions: Any chest pain, tightness, or shortness of breath?
Any recent injury or fall?
Can you raise your arm above your head?
Any sweating or nausea with the pain?

regions.text: Armpit pain most often relates to swollen or tender lymph nodes reacting to a nearby infection (an arm cut, a skin infection, or a cold), a skin condition such as folliculitis or hidradenitis suppurativa, or a pulled muscle. A firm, painless, and enlarging lump is worth medical attention rather than home care.
common_conditions: Reactive lymphadenopathy (swollen node from a nearby infection)
red_flags: A hard, fixed, or rapidly growing lump
Lymph node swelling lasting more than two weeks with no clear cause
Unexplained weight loss or night sweats alongside the swelling
Spreading redness, warmth, or fever (possible infection)
suggested_questions: Can you feel a lump, and has it been growing?
Any recent cut, shave, or skin infection nearby?
Any fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss?
Is the skin red, warm, or draining fluid?

regions.text: Elbow pain commonly comes from tendon overuse (tennis elbow or golfer's elbow), nerve irritation at the 'funny bone', joint inflammation, or an injury such as a fall onto an outstretched arm.
red_flags: Visible deformity after a fall or injury
Inability to bend or straighten the arm
Numbness in the ring and little fingers
Significant swelling with fever (possible joint infection)
suggested_questions: Any recent injury or repetitive strain (lifting, racquet sports)?
Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
Can you fully bend and straighten the elbow?
Any swelling, warmth, or redness?

red_flags: Visible deformity after a fall or injury

suggested_questions: Any recent injury or repetitive strain (lifting, racquet sports)?
Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
Can you fully bend and straighten the elbow?
Any swelling, warmth, or redness?

regions.text: Wrist pain is often from repetitive strain, carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression), ligament sprains, or a fracture, especially after a fall onto an outstretched hand, where a scaphoid fracture can be easily missed on first exam.
red_flags: Deformity or significant swelling after a fall
Numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers
Inability to move the wrist
Persistent pain after a fall even with a normal-looking X-ray (scaphoid fractures are easy to miss early)
suggested_questions: Did you fall onto your hand recently?
Any numbness or tingling in your fingers, especially at night?
Any weakness gripping objects?
Does the pain worsen with wrist movement or repetitive motion?

Any weakness gripping objects?
Does the pain worsen with wrist movement or repetitive motion?

regions.text: Pain in the hand or fingers can come from joint conditions like arthritis, tendon problems such as trigger finger, nerve irritation, or an injury, including cuts and bites, which carry an infection risk in the hand's tight tissue spaces.
red_flags: Visible deformity after an injury
Inability to move a finger
Loss of sensation in a finger
Redness, warmth, or pus after a cut or bite (hand infections can spread quickly)
suggested_questions: Any recent injury, cut, or bite?
Which finger or fingers are affected?
Any numbness or loss of sensation?
Any locking or catching when you bend the finger?

Any numbness or loss of sensation?
Any locking or catching when you bend the finger?

regions.text: Thigh pain is most often a muscle strain or cramp, but it can also come from nerve compression (sciatica referred from the lower back), a blood clot in the leg, or irritation of the IT band along the outer thigh.
common_conditions: Sciatica referred from the lower back
red_flags: Sudden swelling with warmth and tenderness (possible blood clot)
Inability to bear weight
Numbness or weakness down the leg
Pain after a long flight, surgery, or period of immobility
suggested_questions: Any recent exercise, strain, or injury?
Is the thigh swollen or warm to the touch?
Any numbness or weakness down the leg?
Any recent long travel or period of immobility?

Any recent long travel or period of immobility?

regions.text: Knee pain commonly comes from the joint surfaces, the menisci, the surrounding ligaments, or the patellar tendon. Common causes include meniscal tears, ligament sprains, osteoarthritis, and tendinitis from overuse.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight
Sudden severe swelling
A knee that locks or gives way
Visible deformity after an injury
suggested_questions: Any recent injury or twisting motion?
Can you bear weight on the leg?
Any locking, popping, or the knee giving way?
Any swelling or warmth around the knee?

regions.text: Knee pain commonly comes from the joint surfaces, the menisci, the surrounding ligaments, or the patellar tendon. Common causes include meniscal tears, ligament sprains, osteoarthritis, and tendinitis from overuse.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight

suggested_questions: Any recent injury or twisting motion?

regions.text: Shin and calf pain is often muscular (a strain, cramp, or shin splints from running), but a hot, swollen, tender calf can signal a blood clot in the deep veins, which needs urgent attention, especially after travel, surgery, or a period of immobility.
red_flags: A calf that is hot, swollen, and tender, especially after travel, surgery, or immobility (possible blood clot)
Severe pain out of proportion to the injury with tight swelling (possible compartment syndrome)
Sudden inability to bear weight
Numbness or coldness in the foot
suggested_questions: Any recent long travel, surgery, or period of immobility?
Is the calf swollen, warm, or red?
Any numbness or coldness in the foot?
Did the pain start suddenly or build up gradually with activity?

regions.text: Ankle pain is most often a sprain from rolling or twisting the joint, but can also involve the Achilles tendon or, after a significant injury, a fracture.
common_conditions: Gout (sudden severe pain, redness, and swelling)
red_flags: Inability to bear weight at all or take more than a few steps (possible fracture)
Visible deformity
Sudden severe pain, swelling, and redness (possible gout or infection)
A felt or heard 'pop' at the back of the ankle with sudden weakness (possible Achilles rupture)
suggested_questions: Did you twist or roll the ankle?
Can you take a few steps on it?
Any bruising or visible deformity?
Did you feel or hear a pop at the time of injury?

regions.text: Foot and toe pain often relates to the plantar fascia, footwear, overuse, or joint conditions, and is commonly worse with the first steps in the morning (plantar fasciitis) or after a sudden increase in activity (stress fracture).
red_flags: Inability to bear weight
Sudden severe pain, swelling, and redness (possible gout or infection)
Numbness or loss of sensation, especially if diabetic
An open sore or wound that is not healing, especially if diabetic
suggested_questions: Is the pain worse with your first steps in the morning?
Any recent increase in activity or new footwear?
Any numbness, especially if you have diabetes?
Any open sores or wounds on the foot?
